title: How to set up evolving rep ranges (theoretical aspects)
summary: He explains how to design evolving rep ranges (ERR), which vary sets and/or reps session to session. The range must stay narrow enough to cycle quickly and keep forcing weight progression, tonnage swings must be compensated by the rest of the program, reps should stay within 1-12, and static schemes like 3x5 can complement them.

claims.claim: Any scheme that evolves volume and intensity is strictly superior to static 5x5 or 3x5 for manipulation and tonnage control.
Evolving rep ranges can modify sets, reps, or both; possibilities are infinite but only a narrow range is optimal.
The wider the range, the longer it takes to cycle back and add weight, reducing control; an ERR is a microcosm of a hypertrophy block, not a block itself.
An ERR from 2 to 12 reps is too wide because you spend too long at the same weight before returning to 2 reps with more load.
ERRs can be linear (add one rep per workout) or, as he does, rotate sets: 4, then 5,4, then 6,5,4, then 7,5,3, then 8,6,4; once he hits 8,6,4 he restarts at 4 with more weight.
He teaches intensity windows and appropriate volume rather than specific numbers, so you can evaluate any rep scheme yourself.

ERRs are excellent for strength work, and strength work should progress; stalling at the same weight for 4-5 months on a compound means the program is wrong, unless it's a body part you don't want to grow.
Even for bodybuilders, the weight on the bar drives tonnage, which is directly linked to physique change, so ERRs must still push progression as 5x5 and 3x5 do.
Changing sets creates large tonnage swings: going from a single set of 4 to 8,6,4 (18 reps) at similar intensity is a big gap.
He compensates tonnage swings through lifting rotations, accessories on low-volume days, a body part split and high frequency, adding volume e.g. to the lower body two days later.
Minimalist programs need ERRs designed to deliver enough volume on the days they're performed, since no variations follow to fill gaps.
Keep ERR reps within 1-12; above 12 the window gets too wide to return to adding weight.
Track total tonnage (reps x weight), ballparked; there is no optimal rep range so being off by one or two reps doesn't matter.
The essence of ERRs is freedom from repeating the same sets and reps every session.
Keep sets per exercise reasonable; don't do 10 sets of strength work, which lands in an unproductive intensity or volume window and wastes time.
ERRs can be used for all training, but they require constant tracking that some find draining; static ranges like 3x5 or 3x3 can be slotted in because ERRs work around them.
